extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and informed readers interested in poetic theory and criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and composing poetry, and for conducting literary criticism—distinguishing faculties (fancy vs imagination), judging works in context, and prescribing criticly decorum and aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism grounded in fixed canons
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviews should be conducted on far other principles, and with far other motives; the reviewers support their decisions by reference to fixed canons of criticism, previously established and deduced from the nature of man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid arbitrary dictation and petulant sneers; base judgments on established, philosophically grounded principles rather than personal caprice or pique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critic should elucidate beauties, not only defects
rubrics_metrics.description: He who tells me that there are defects in a new work, tells me nothing which I should not have taken for granted without his information. But he, who points out and elucidates the beauties of an original work does indeed give me interesting information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize exposition of an author's merits because that imparts useful, non-obvious information to readers; avoid critiques that merely enumerate defects without positive explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not judge a poet by accidental failures or isolated passages
rubrics_metrics.description: I know nothing that surpasses the vileness of deciding on the merits of a poet or painter ... by accidental failures or faulty passages; except the impudence of defending it, as the proper duty, and most instructive part, of criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating minor faults as determinative of an artist's overall merit; do not let isolated lapses eclipse characteristic beauties; weigh characteristic defects as pointers to strengths where genius exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid amplifying faults by reprinting them
rubrics_metrics.description: If in a volume of poetry the critic should find poem or passage which he deems more especially worthless, he is sure to select and reprint it in the review; by which, on his own grounds, he wastes as much more paper than the author ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reprinting and publicizing the worst passages defeats the critic's professed purpose and spreads the very material they condemn; this is a hypocritical and ludicrous anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Playful or trifling compositions are legitimate if not immoral
rubrics_metrics.description: But on the other hand, I conceive, that Mr. Southey was quite unable to comprehend, wherein could consist the crime or mischief of printing half a dozen or more playful poems ... provided they contained nothing immoral. In the present age periturae parcere chartae is emphatically an unreasonable demand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not demand that every printed work aim at high or permanent ends; light, occasional, or playful pieces have rightful claims to publication so long as they are not immoral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider authorial intent and context when judging works
rubrics_metrics.description: The humbler passages in the poems themselves were dwelt on and cited to justify the rejection of the theory. What in and for themselves would have been either forgotten or forgiven as imperfections, or at least comparative failures, provoked direct hostility when announced as intentional, as the result of choice after full deliberation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism should account for prefatory statements, declared aims, and the intended design of a work; intentional stylistic choices should be evaluated differently than accidental lapses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate collections by their aggregate merit, not by a few inferior pieces
rubrics_metrics.description: The poems, therefore, at the worst, could only be regarded as so many light or inferior coins in a rouleau of gold, not as so much alloy in a weight of bullion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat minor or inferior poems within a collection as small losses amid greater achievements; avoid letting a few weaker items invalidate the whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the influence of framing (prefaces, publicity) on reception
rubrics_metrics.description: In the critical remarks, therefore, prefixed and annexed to the Lyrical Ballads, I believe, we may safely rest, as the true origin of the unexampled opposition which Mr. Wordsworth’s writings have been since doomed to encounter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that prefatory essays, publicity, or pointed framing can provoke or direct criticism; evaluate whether reaction stems from the work itself or from its announced theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish between 'seductive faults' and simple affectations
rubrics_metrics.description: The seductive faults, the dulcia vitia of Cowley, Marini, or Darwin might reasonably be thought capable of corrupting the public judgment ... But that a downright simpleness, under the affectation of simplicity, prosaic words in feeble metre ... should succeed in forming a school of imitators ... this is indeed matter of wonder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess both the nature and long-term danger of faults: some 'seductive' faults can mislead imitators for generations, while mere prosaic affectations may be less pernicious though often overcritically vilified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry should avoid excessive obscurity that demands undue close attention
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelty and struggling crowd of images, acting in conjunction with the difficulties of the style, demands always a greater closeness of attention, than poetry ... has a right to claim. It not seldom therefore justified the complaint of obscurity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While richness of image is valuable, style should not be so knotty or contorted that comprehension requires disproportionate effort; aim for clarity appropriate to poetic genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union of deep feeling with profound thought as a mark of excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: It was the union of deep feeling with profound thought; the fine balance of truth in observing, with the imaginative faculty in modifying, the objects observed; and above all the original gift of spreading the tone, the atmosphere, and with it the depth and height of the ideal world around forms, incidents, and situations ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek a balance: genuine feeling married to intellectual depth; truthful observation imaginatively transformed; the poet’s power to establish tone and an immersive ideal atmosphere is a key criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'false taste' — hackneyed, arbitrary, or illogical phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: And above all the occasional obscurities, which had risen from an imperfect control over the resources of his native language, had almost wholly disappeared, together with that worse defect of arbitrary and illogical phrases, at once hackneyed and fantastic, which hold so distinguished a place in the technique of ordinary poetry ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steer clear of clichés, forced or illogical turns of phrase and fantastical jargon that masquerades as originality; polish language control to remove these faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate fancy from imagination in analysis and production
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated meditations led me first to suspect ... that Fancy and Imagination were two distinct and widely different faculties ... To the faculty by which I had characterized Milton, we should confine the term ‘imagination;’ while the other would be contra-distinguished as ‘fancy.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'imagination' for the higher, shaping, creative faculty (Miltonian); reserve 'fancy' for the lower associative or merely ornamental faculty (Cowley); this taxonomy should inform both criticism and poetic practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admire on principle to imitate without losing originality
rubrics_metrics.description: To admire on principle, is the only way to imitate without loss of originality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics and poets should cultivate principled admiration—understanding underlying principles of greatness enables emulation that preserves originality rather than mere copying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for development: early faults may be transient markers of growth
rubrics_metrics.description: The poetic Psyche, in its process to full development, undergoes as many changes as its Greek namesake ... genius clears and purifies itself from the faults and errors of its earliest products ... faults ... constitute the very ferment, by which themselves are carried off.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging a poet, consider career stage: early 'ferment' or unevenness can be developmental; critics should not conflate youthful faults with permanent incapacity.
